title: More complex than it looks
hookLine: kamma is not one-to-one; don't generalize from a single case

lines: TWO PACKS A DAY. LIVED TO NINETY-FIVE.
cards: Somebody's uncle smoked two packs a day and lived to ninety-five. So, he says at every family dinner, smoking can't be that bad. One case, one big conclusion.
The hundred and thirty-sixth discourse is about exactly this mistake, made by serious spiritual seekers.
It opens with a misunderstanding: a wanderer named Potaliputta tells the monk Samiddhi a claim about what the Buddha teaches, Samiddhi answers too simply, and Ananda brings it all to the Buddha.
So the Buddha lays out the whole thing carefully.

teach.b: Four people, the Buddha says. The first harms living beings, steals, lies, and after death is reborn in a bad state. The second does the same and is reborn in a good state.
The third lives well and is reborn in a good state. The fourth lives well and is reborn in a bad state. Now imagine a meditator with a special power of vision who sees just one of these cases.
Seeing the second, they conclude: there are no bad deeds; nothing comes of them. Seeing the fourth: good living is pointless.
Seeing the first: everyone who harms goes to a bad state, always, and anyone who says otherwise is wrong. The Buddha agrees with what they saw. He disagrees with what they concluded.

They saw a real case and turned it into a universal law. The person who harmed and still went to a good state, he says, may have done good deeds earlier, or later, or held a clear and right view at the time of death.
The harmful deeds will still ripen, sometime. The same in reverse for the good person in a bad state.
Deeds ripen on their own timing, mixed with everything else a person has done.

teach.h: DEEDS RIPEN ON THEIR OWN TIME
teach.b: So yesterday's teaching isn't a vending machine: put in a deed, get a matching result today.
It's more like weather, built from many currents at once. The Buddha didn't deny the pattern. He denied the shortcut: one case, one law, and a quick verdict on a stranger.

how: MN 135 and MN 136 sit side by side in the collection and are studied as a pair; another discourse (AN 4.77) lists the results of kamma among the things not to be speculated about.

o: action, a deed that ripens in its own time
a reward or punishment handed out by a god
fate fixed at birth that can't be changed

games.q: four people, four outcomes: tap the pairs.
p: the monk who answered too simply

s: in MN 136 the Buddha says the seers' visions were false
he agrees with what they saw, and disagrees with the sweeping conclusions they drew.
the discourse describes someone who lived well and still had a bad rebirth
the fourth person: earlier deeds, or a wrong view at death, may explain it.
MN 136 says harmful deeds can come to nothing
they will still ripen sometime, on their own timing.

games.q: a seer with special vision watches a harmful person be reborn in a good state. what does the seer conclude, in MN 136?
o: there are no bad deeds; nothing comes of them.
the person must have done good earlier or later.
games.why: the seer jumps from one case to a universal law. the Buddha explains other deeds may have ripened first, and the harm will still ripen sometime.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose life you've summed up in one sentence: they got lucky, they had it coming, they never try. Hold that sentence up and ask what you haven't seen, what came before, what might come after.
You don't need the answer; let the sentence loosen a little, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kamma. Action, deed: it isn't one-to-one, deeds ripen on their own time, and one case seen clearly is still only one case. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kamma: action, deed. Sanskrit karma. the subject of MN 135 and MN 136.

carryVoice: Your line: one case, not one law. What someone saw can be true even when the rule they made from it isn't. Day five hundred two, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 136, Mahakammavibhanga Sutta (the greater exposition of action)
Anguttara Nikaya 4.77, Acinteyya Sutta (the four unthinkables)
